Goal

The purpose of this guide is to explain the underlying tech and logic used to deploy a scheduling agent, Cal.ai, in production using LangChain.

Context

Recently, our team at Rubric Labs had the opportunity to build Cal.com's AI-driven email assistant. For context, we're a team of builders who love to tackle challenging engineering problems.

The vision for the project was to simplify the complex world of calendar management. Some of the core features we had in mind included:

Turning informal emails into bookings: "Want to meet tomorrow at 2?"

Listing and rearranging bookings: "Cancel my next meeting"

Answering basic questions: "How does my Tuesday look?"

and more. In summary, we wanted to build a personal, AI-powered scheduling assistant that can offer a complete suite of CRUD operations to the end user, all within the confines of their email client using natural language.

Architecture

We decided to achieve this using an AI agent, particularly an OpenAI functions agent which is better at dealing with structured data, given Cal.com's API exposes a set of booking operations with clear inputs. The underlying architecture is explained below.

Agent architecture. A scratchpad is a type of memory where the AI writes to itself.

Here we also make additional checks, such as ensuring that the email is from a Cal.com user to prevent misuse. After the email has been verified and parsed, it is passed to the agent loop.

Agent

The agent is a LangChain OpenAI functions agent which uses fine-tuned versions of GPT models. This agent is passed pre-defined functions or tools and is able to detect when a function should to be called. This allows us to specify the required inputs and desired output.

Tools — a tool is simply a Javascript function with a name, description, and input schema

Chat model — a chat model is a variation of an LLM model that uses an interface where "chat messages" are the inputs and outputs

In addition to the tools and the chat model, we also pass a prefix prompt to add context for the model. Let's look into each of the inputs.

Prompt

The prompt is an opportunity to direct the model by providing context. The user's relevant information (userId, user.username, user.timezone, etc.) is used to construct a prompt which is passed to the agent.

You are Cal.ai - a bleeding edge scheduling assistant that interfaces via email. Make sure your final answers are definitive, complete and well formatted. Sometimes, tools return errors. In this case, try to handle the error intelligently or ask the user for more information. Tools will always handle times in UTC, but times sent to users should be formatted per that user's timezone.

Deployment

We like to work at the edge of technology. That extends to our APIs. Luckily, LangChain.js apps run well in serverless environments. Offering Cal.ai to thousands of users is as simple as serving the LangChain app via a Next.js endpoint hosted on Vercel. What a time to be alive.

Imagine having a friend who could help you with homework, answer all your questions instantly, play your favorite music, set reminders, and even tell jokes! Sounds amazing, right? Well, there are already such friends around, except they aren't humans—they're called AI Assistants! These incredible tools use something called Artificial Intelligence, or simply AI, to become our helpful companions. But how exactly does this work? Let's dive into understanding AI Assistants together!

**Section 1: What Are AI Assistants?**

Inventors have always tried to create machines that can mimic or enhance human abilities. Think of cars, airplanes, or dishwashers – these are all inventions made to simplify tasks for us. Now imagine if a machine could understand speech, recognize images, solve complex problems, or even write poetry! This would open up endless possibilities for helping people every day. That's where AI comes in.

An AI Assistant is a software program designed to assist users by performing various tasks based on their commands or requests. They live inside smart speakers, smartphones, laptops, and other devices, waiting patiently for you to ask them something. When activated, AI Assistants listen carefully, process your request using advanced mathematical algorithms, and then respond accordingly. All this happens almost instantaneously! Some popular AI Assistants you might know are Siri, Alexa, Google Assistant, and Cortana.

**Section 2: How Does An AI Assistant Work?**

To build an AI Assistant, engineers borrow concepts from neuroscience, creating networks inspired by the structure of our brains. These networks consist of layers upon layers of tiny computing units known as neurons. Each layer takes in some information, processes it slightly differently, and passes it along until eventually, the entire system produces an output. Together, these interconnected neurons form what's called a Neural Network.

Let's consider an example involving image recognition: Suppose you want your AI Assistant to identify different breeds of dogs. You would first train the Neural Network by feeding it thousands of pictures labeled with specific dog breeds. Over time, the network starts recognizing patterns within those images, learning subtle differences between one breed and another. Eventually, after many rounds of training, the AI Assistant becomes proficient at identifying dog breeds just by looking at photos!

Similarly, when dealing with voice commands, AI Assistants convert spoken words into written text through a process called Speech Recognition. Then, Natural Language Processing techniques analyze the meaning behind the words before finally executing the appropriate action. Whether playing songs, setting alarms, or answering trivia questions, AI Assistants rely heavily on complex mathematics and intricate programming to serve us effectively.

**Section 3: Benefits And Concerns Of AI Assistants**

Just like any invention, AI Assistants bring numerous benefits and challenges alike. On the positive side, they save time, provide easy accessibility, and cater to diverse needs. Imagine being able to control multiple appliances at home using only your voice or asking your assistant to read out recipes while cooking. Furthermore, AI Assistants offer tremendous potential in fields like education, healthcare, entertainment, and more.

Since AI Assistants often require constant internet connectivity and access to personal data, safeguarding user information becomes crucial. Moreover, striking a balance between utilizing AI Assistants and maintaining genuine social connections remains essential. As thoughtful future innovators, considering both aspects allows us to harness technology responsibly and ethically.

What exactly is an AI Assistant?
----------------------------------

An AI assistant is a type of software program designed to interact with humans using natural language processing, which is just a fancy way of saying they understand when we talk to them like we would speak to another person. How do AI Assistants work?
--------------------------

At the heart of every AI assistant lies machine learning algorithms, complex mathematical models that enable the system to learn from data over time. When you first start talking to your AI buddy, it doesn't know much about you or how to respond appropriately. ### Speech Recognition

First, the AI assistant must convert spoken words into written text so it can analyze and interpret the command. This is done through a technology called automatic speech recognition (ASR), which uses statistical methods to match sounds to corresponding words within its vocabulary.

### Natural Language Processing

Once the AI assistant has converted speech to text, it then analyzes the input using natural language processing techniques. This involves understanding grammar, syntax, context, and intent behind the user's request. By doing so, the AI assistant can determine whether you want to hear a joke, check the weather forecast, or call your best friend.

### Knowledge Representation

Next, the AI assistant retrieves relevant information based on your query. It does this by searching databases, accessing online resources, or tapping into pre-programmed facts stored in its memory banks. All this information is organized logically, allowing the AI assistant to provide accurate answers swiftly.

### Reasoning and Decision Making

After gathering all necessary details, the AI assistant decides on the most appropriate response based on various factors such as relevance, urgency, and past interactions with you. Sometimes, it will also use reasoning skills to draw conclusions from available data and offer suggestions or recommendations accordingly.

### Text-to-Speech Conversion

Finally, once the AI assistant determines the perfect reply, it converts the text back into spoken words using a technique called text-to-speech synthesis. This allows the AI assistant to communicate verbally, ensuring smooth conversation flow between human and machine.

Overview

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a transformative technology that simulates human intelligence in machines, enabling them to perform tasks that typically require human intellect. This includes learning from experiences, understanding complex content, recognizing speech, making decisions, and solving problems. For beginners, it's essential to understand the basic concepts such as machine learning, neural networks, natural language processing (NLP), generative AI, and AI detectors. These foundational elements empower computers to process and analyze vast amounts of data, learn patterns, and mimic human-like interactions, making AI integral in various fields such as healthcare, finance, customer service, and more.

Why is understanding AI important?

Understanding AI is crucial because it's rapidly becoming a part of our daily lives, transforming industries, and shaping the future of work. Knowledge of AI enables individuals to leverage its capabilities, anticipate its impact on society, and contribute to its ethical development.

What is machine learning?

Machine learning is a subset of AI that involves the development of algorithms allowing computers to learn from and make predictions or decisions based on data. It's the backbone of AI's decision-making capabilities.

How do neural networks work?

Neural networks are designed to mimic the human brain's structure and function, enabling AI systems to recognize patterns and solve problems in a way that's similar to human thinking. They consist of layers of nodes that process input data and can learn from it over time.

What is natural language processing (NLP)?

NLP is a field of AI focused on the interaction between computers and humans using natural language. It allows machines to read, decipher, understand, and make sense of human languages in a valuable way, facilitating tasks like translation and sentiment analysis.

What are generative AI and its applications?

Generative AI refers to AI models, like GPT and DALL-E, that can generate new content, including text, images, or music, that resembles human-created content. Its applications range from creating realistic images from textual descriptions to generating human-like text responses.

Understanding the Basics of AI

Before diving deep into the world of AI, it's crucial to grasp the fundamentals. When we talk about 'how does AI work', we're essentially discussing algorithms and machine learning models that enable computers to make decisions, learn from data, and mimic human intelligence. Start by exploring the basic concepts of machine learning, neural networks, and natural language processing (NLP). These are the building blocks of AI that allow machines to process and understand human language, solve complex problems, and even create content.

Explore Machine Learning Models

Begin with machine learning models. These are algorithms that learn from data over time, improving their accuracy in tasks such as image recognition, speech recognition, and language translation. There are various resources online, including courses and tutorials, that can provide a solid foundation in understanding these models.

Delve Into Neural Networks

Neural networks are inspired by the human brain's structure and are crucial in enabling AI to process complex patterns and data. Familiarize yourself with the basics of neural networks, including how they are structured and how they learn from data. This knowledge is key to understanding more advanced AI applications.

Understand Natural Language Processing (NLP)

NLP is a field of AI that focuses on the interaction between computers and humans using natural language. It's what allows AI to understand, interpret, and generate human language. Getting a grip on NLP principles will help you understand how AI can perform tasks like sentiment analysis, language translation, and content creation.

Deciphering AI in Texting and Communication

When we ask, 'what does AI mean in texting', we're not just talking about shorthand or acronyms. AI in texting often refers to chatbots, virtual assistants, and other AI-driven technologies that can understand and mimic human conversation. To get hands-on with AI in texting, start experimenting with AI chatbots or virtual assistants. Many platforms allow you to create or interact with chatbots, giving you a practical understanding of how AI can understand and generate human-like responses.

Experiment with AI Chatbots

Create or interact with AI chatbots on platforms like Telegram, Slack, or custom websites. Pay attention to how these chatbots understand your queries and respond in a conversational manner. This will give you insight into the practical applications of NLP in AI.

Analyze Virtual Assistants

Use virtual assistants like Siri, Google Assistant, or Alexa. Observe how they process your voice commands, understand context, and provide relevant responses or actions. This experience will deepen your understanding of AI's capabilities in natural language understanding and generation.

Unraveling How Generative AI Works

Generative AI is a fascinating area that focuses on creating content, whether it's text, images, or music, that is indistinguishable from content created by humans. To understand 'how does generative AI works', delve into technologies like GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) and DALL-E. How do you give someone a hand-on introduction to MicroBlocks if they don't have a microcontroller board?

That's a problem we have encountered many times when presenting MicroBlocks at virtual workshops over the past several years. It is also a problem faced by teachers who don't have enough boards for every student in their class.

Enter Boardie, a virtual board for MicroBlocks that lets people try MicroBlocks right in the browser.

The goal of Boardie is to introduce MicroBlocks to people who are thinking about physical computing but don't yet have a board. We want to help them see that coding a microcontroller is easy and fun, and encourage them to dive into actual physical computing.

What Boardie is not

Boardie is not meant to replace a real microcontroller. The magic of physical computing arises from its ability to interact with the physical world: to sense physical phenomenon like light, sound, and temperature and to control things like lights, motors, and electrical appliances.

Boardie makes no attempt to simulate physical sensors or output devices. While it is not difficult to simulate those things — for example, sliders can be used as virtual sensor inputs and animated images can show virtual motors and servos — we feel that doing that misses the point.

We want people to experience the magic, and the resulting learning, of doing physical computing in the actual physical world.

What Boardie is

Boardie is a virtual board that does some of the things that actual microcontrollers can do. It has two programmable buttons, like a micro:bit, and it can emulate the 5x5 LED display of the micro:bit or the 240x240 pixel TFT display of the Adafruit Clue. It can make square-wave beeps and play tunes, and it supports a simple file system. Finally, it supports the same MicroBlocks HTTP client library that works on WiFi enabled boards.

Using Boardie

Boardie runs in the MicroBlocks web app at microblocks.fun/run. Since it does not require WebSerial, it can run in Safari and Firefox, as well as Chrome and Edge. Boardie is not supported in the MicroBlocks stand-alone apps.

Start Boardie by clicking on the USB icon and selecting open Boardie. When Boardie is open, MicroBlocks is connected to it and you can program and interact with it in the same way you would a real, physical device.

MicroBlocks can only be connected to one board at a time. So, since Boardie is a virtual board, you'll need to disconnect Boardie before connecting MicroBlocks to a physical board. Use the disconnect command in the USB icon menu or Boardie's power switch to disconnect. Boardie disappears when it is disconnected.

Examples

Here is a simple micro:bit example running on Boardie, the Heartbeat project:

Clicking the A button on Boardie runs the script.

When the Boardie device is in focus you can also use the left and right arrow keys or the A and B keys on your keyboard to activate the buttons. That feature is useful for games.

Having a TFT display means we're not limited to a 5x5 matrix. As with the Adafruit Clue, the Citilab ED1 or the M5Stack, you can draw arbitrary graphics on the screen using the MicroBlocks TFT library.

This Jumpy Ball game was originally designed for the Citilab ED1 but is coded to automatically adjust to different screen dimensions:

Boardie features a ~5MB file system that can store data or media files. This tile-matching memory game uses the MicroBlocks BMP library to display images:

You may have noticed that the Boardie TFT screen is actually a touch screen, which gives you more possibilities for UI design than just the two buttons would.

Boardie also features a speaker. The speaker grill at the bottom of the face plate glows when sound is being played:

Here's the exact same game being playing on a physical board:

We can't wait to see what you will create with Boardie!

Boardie Specs

For the more tech-oriented, here are the technical specs of this virtual board:

RAM: 65kB

File storage: ~5MB

Inputs: A and B buttons, plus a combined A+B button, touch screen

Outputs: 240x240px 24-bit TFT, speaker

Network capabilities: HTTP Client

Acknowledgment

Many thanks to Christiane, leader of the SAP Young Thinkers group, for suggesting Boardie. This will ensure people maximize their time and effort to help reach their goals for any event.", "truncated": false, "original_chars": 325, "returned_chars": 325}, {"rank": 8, "id": "shard_04136_43648", "docid": "shard_04136_43648", "kind": "document", "rrf_score": 0.015625, "text": "Photographic memory, instant artworks, instantaneous translation, lifelike virtual reality and much more are all coming to your pocket.

IPhone owners will get an upgrade on September 13 that allows them to find a picture of nearly anyone or anything, anywhere and from any time. Neural network artificial intelligence in the new iOS 10 performs 11 billion calculations in a tenth of a second on each photo snapped to figure out who people are and even what mood they're in.

advertisement

advertisement

iOS 10's new Photos app is only the latest example of a growing movement toward handheld artificial intelligence. Aipoly, an app released in January, recognizes objects and speaks their names aloud to blind people. Google Translate can replace text in one language with another language as soon as you point your camera at it. All this happens even if you can't get cell reception.

Aipoly identified not only the animal, but the breed. It says the name aloud and displays it.

Just as "the cloud" was becoming the answer to every "How does it work?" question, smartphones have started clawing back their independence, performing on their own tasks that used to require a tether to a server farm. The result is a more natural AI experience, without the annoying or creepy lag of an internet connection to a data center. "If I said, 'Hey Siri, what is this?' it would take two seconds to send a picture to the cloud [and get a response back]," says Aipoly
cofounder Alberto Rizzoli. "It kinda feels like talking to someone who just woke up." Aipoly was not the first seeing app for the blind; it was the first to identify objects instantly by cutting its dependence on the cloud and running AI on a phone.

Such instantaneous AI will take augmented reality far beyond Pokémon Go by accurately mapping the surroundings in detail to insert rich 3D objects, characters, and animations into the video feed on a phone or tablet screen. Likewise, virtual reality will start looking more genuine with mobile AI, according to Gary Brotman, director of product management at mobile chip maker Qualcomm, where he heads the machine learning platform. "To do that right, everything has to be totally realtime," he says. "So you have to be able to present the video, present the audio, and have the intelligence that drives the eye-tracking, the head tracking, gesture tracking, and spatial audio tracking so you can map the acoustics of the room to that virtual experience."

advertisement

This behind-the-scenes view shows how Aipoly rapidly considers the likelihood of different options.

AI will also drive convenience features. You might see virtual assistants that use the phone's camera to recognize where you are, such as a specific street or the inside of a restaurant, and bring up relevant apps, says Rizzoli. And for once, such hyper-conveniences may not have the creep factor. If future AI doesn't need the cloud, then the cloud doesn't need your personal data.

"For privacy reasons, for latency reasons, for a variety of others, there's no reason why the locus of control for analytics and intelligence shouldn't be on the [phone]," says Brotman.

"People want better mobile games on their phones and their iPads," says Rizzoli. "So Apple has been particularly good, and so has Qualcomm and the other chip manufacturers, in making better performance." That's pushed the development of more powerful mobile CPUs and Graphics Processing Units. While CPUs mostly work sequentially, GPUs work in parallel on the simpler but very numerous tasks required for quickly rendering 3D graphics. AI also requires performing multiple straightforward duties in tandem.

Take what's called a "convolutional neural network"—a staple of modern image recognition. Modeled on how the brain's visual cortex works, CNNs divide the visual field into overlapping tiles and then, in tandem, filter out simple details such as edges from all of these tiles. That info goes to another layer of neurons (biological in humans or virtual in software), which might combine edges into lines; another layer might recognize primitive shapes. Each layer (of which their may be dozens) further refines the perception of the image. "You're looking at a photo, and you're identifying various elements of it at the same time," says Rizzoli. "You're identifying edges, and you're identifying what shapes [might exist]. And all of this can be done in parallel."

Google Translate in action

Smartphone chips have been up to the challenge for a few years. Even 2013's iPhone 5s supports the new people, scene, and object recognition upgrade in iOS 10; and Aipoly is working on versions that will run on the iPhone 5 as well as Android phones going back several years. But programmers have just recently been taking advantage of this power. Photo effects app Prisma, which launched in June, has been one of the early adopters.

advertisement

Twenty-five-year-old Aleksey Moiseenkov created the app, which renders a smartphone photo in a choice of over 30 artistic styles, such as "The Scream," "Mondrian," and many with playful titles like "Illegal Beauty," "Flame Thrower," and "#GetUrban." The effects are rendered nearly instantaneously, which belies their complexity. An Instagram filter simply tweaks basic parameters like color, contrast, brightness, or white balance in pre-set amounts. Prisma has to analyze the image, recognize elements like shapes, lines, colors, and shading, and redraw it from scratch like Edvard Munch or Piet Mondrian might. The results can be gorgeous, making even a banal picture intriguing.

Prisma initially did all this work in the cloud, but Moiseenkov says that could hurt the quality of the app. "We have a lot of users in Asia," he says, "and we need to give the same experience no matter what the connection is, wherever the server or cloud processing is." A new version of the iPhone app that came out in August runs entirely on the phone, and Moiseenkov is working on the same shift for the Android version.

An upgrade that applies the same artistic effects to video is coming, too, possibly in September, says Moiseenkov. "Video is much more complicated in terms of overloading the servers and all that stuff," he says, so doing effects right on the phone is crucial.

advertisement

An upcoming version of Prisma transform video as well as photos.

Moiseenkov and his team had to figure out from scratch how to get their AI software working on smartphones, but future programmers might have an easier time. In May, Qualcomm came out with a software developer's kit called the "Neural Processing Engine" for its Snapdragon 820 chip, which powers 2016's high-end Android phones, like the Samsung Galaxy S7 and Note 7, Moto Z and Z Force, OnePlus 3, HTC 10, and LG G5. The software juggles tasks between the CPU, GPU, and other components of the chip for jobs like scene detection, text recognition, face recognition, and natural language processing (understanding conversational speech rather than just rigid commands).

Using only about one watt of power, the Myriad 2 would be thrifty enough to run in a phone, too. Movidius has made a few vague statements about future products. In June, it announced "a strategic partnership to provide advanced vision processing technology to a variety of VR-centric Lenovo products." These could be VR headsets or phones, or both. Back in January, Movidius and Google announced a collaboration "to accelerate the adoption of deep learning within mobile devices." I asked Movidius and Google about the deals, but they wouldn't say anything more.

Apple has been characteristically coy about its AI plans, not saying much before it previewed iOS 10 in June.

The AI-powered Photos app is the biggest component. It uses neural networks for the deep learning process that recognizes scenes, objects, and faces in pictures to group them and make them searchable. Its Memories feature puts together collections of pictures and videos based on people in them, places or what it judges to be a significant event, like a trip. Doing all this work on the phone keeps personal information private, says Apple.

AI-generated Memories collections in iOS 10

Neural networks also power Apple's predictive typing that helps finish sentences, and AI appeared well before iOS 10. Apple switched Siri over to a neural network running on the phone back in July 2014 to improve its speech recognition.

advertisement

Siri is how most app makers will plug into the iPhone's AI, for now. Apple hasn't released AI-programming tools for its A series chips the way Qualcomm has for Snapdragon, but a feature called SiriKit lets developers connect their apps so people can interact with the apps by chatting with Apple's virtual assistant.

And Apple may not be far behind Qualcomm in helping third-party developers leverage AI. It recently spent a reported $200 million on a company called Turi that makes AI tools for programmers. Developers will have more power to work with, too. The new A10 Fusion chip in the iPhone 7 and 7 Plus has a CPU that runs 40% faster than in the previous generation iPhones, and the graphics run 50% faster.

As artificial intelligence continues expanding across the tech world, it seems destined to grow on phones, too. Expectations are rising that gadgets will simply know what we want and what we mean. "I can say that the large percentage of mobile apps will become AI apps," says Nardo Manaloto, an AI engineer and consultant focused on health care apps like virtual medical assistants.

advertisement

Alberto Rizzoli expects to see a lot of new apps by CES in January. App creators "will follow…when more tools for deep-learning software become available, and the developers themselves become more aware of it," he says. "It's still considered to be a dark magic by a lot of computer science people…And it's not."

The following three concepts extend the pattern seen in Cal.ai's photo-based calorie tracking, Boardy.ai's relationship-building agent, and calendar tools like Reclaim and Clockwise, each pushing further into agentic, multimodal AI that gets structurally better as foundation models improve rather than just wrapping a chatbot around an app. The first idea is a proactive "AI chief of staff" that captures a user's meetings and conversations through a small always-on wearable, builds a personal knowledge graph, and executes tasks across a user's tools instead of only summarizing. Technically it would need a dedicated capture device, because mobile operating systems suspend the microphone during calls and app backgrounding, a constraint that already forced the Limitless pendant, formerly Rewind, to move from software to hardware to keep an always-available microphone. Captured context would be embedded into a vector store and reasoned over by an LLM agent built with function-calling and tool orchestration, the same architectural pattern used to build Cal.com's own Cal.ai email scheduling bot, which runs an OpenAI-functions LangChain agent with a scratchpad memory over Cal.com's booking API, deployed serverlessly on Vercel. Instead of stopping at a recap, the agent would draft follow-up emails, update a CRM, and reschedule conflicts, mirroring Limitless's own roadmap toward native Slack integration, drafted messages, and "agents that can take actions on behalf of users." The problem it solves is that people forget most of what they experience within a week and waste hours on busywork after every conversation, and the product removes that busywork while keeping the user present. Direct competitors include Limitless/Rewind for capture and memory, and natural-language scheduling agents like Reclaim, Clockwise, and the email-based assistant Clara, which show users already want calendar and task actions triggered by plain-language requests. The technical moat is that as multimodal models get cheaper and better at long-context reasoning, the agent can chain more autonomous multi-tool actions across a person's digital life than today's narrow single-tool automations, a shift Limitless's own roadmap signals is only beginning. Virality mirrors how Clara's recipients experience it: non-users receive the agent's emails or shared recaps directly, an acquisition loop rather than a marketing expense. The second idea is a "metabolic twin" that fuses a continuous glucose monitor, computer-vision food logging, and wearable sleep and activity data into a forecasting agent that predicts blood-sugar spikes before they happen and can act on the prediction. The closest existing product, Signos, already pairs a Dexcom G6 or G7 monitor with an AI app that learns a personalized "optimal glucose range" and coaches in real time, having raised a $20 million Series B backed by GV and Dexcom Ventures. Photo-based food logging already works today in apps like MyBuddy AI Coach, which uses computer vision to identify ingredients and portion sizes from a single photo to compute calories and macros. The gap this idea targets is explicit in a firsthand Signos review: the app sends "Fast Rise" alerts, but "the app itself won't facilitate learning or implement lifestyle adjustments on your behalf," leaving interpretation to the user. A more ambitious version would fuse the CGM time-series, vision-based meal log, and wearable data into one model that forecasts a spike before the first bite and proactively suggests a substitution, closing the loop today's dashboards leave open. This matters because over 96 million Americans are prediabetic, and CGMs are moving from a diabetes tool into a consumer category, as shown by competitors NutriSense, Veri, Levels, and Dexcom's own over-the-counter Stelo sensor. The moat compounds as vision models improve at fine-grained portion estimation and forecasting-oriented architectures mature, shifting the category from reactive dashboards to genuinely predictive coaching. The third idea is a consumer "autonomous advocate" that places real phone calls on a user's behalf to cancel subscriptions, dispute charges, and negotiate bills, using a live voice agent rather than scripted IVR menus. The core mechanism already exists in enterprise form: programmable voice APIs chain speech-to-text, an LLM reasoning over the transcript, and text-to-speech, letting an AI converse naturally on a call. Bland AI's enterprise product shows the needed pieces, including fine-tuning a custom model on a company's own call transcripts, injecting live external API data mid-call, and chaining calls to spreadsheets through Zapier, exposed via a simple developer API. DoNotPay proved the negotiation use case directly, cloning founder Joshua Browder's voice with Resemble.ai and combining GPT-J for live responses with GPT-3.5-driven scripts to automate refund negotiations with companies like Southwest Airlines. The problem is that today's alternative, Rocket Money, only negotiates bills by taking 30 to 60 percent of first-year savings and still leans on human-in-the-loop negotiation rather than a fully autonomous agent working purely for the user. Other voice-agent competitors like PolyAI, Calldesk, Simple Phones, and Echowin focus on business customer-service call handling rather than consumer-side advocacy, leaving the personal-advocate niche largely open. The moat is tied directly to foundation-model progress: GPT-4o processes voice, text, and vision through one end-to-end network at roughly 320-millisecond latency, versus the multi-second lag of earlier cascaded Twilio-plus-ChatGPT pipelines, and as native speech-to-speech models keep closing that gap, this agent becomes indistinguishable from a human caller. Growth would come from users sharing concrete savings outcomes and from an API-first architecture, similar to Bland's per-minute developer API, letting the advocate be embedded directly into banking apps for distribution. Across all three, the common thread is choosing problems where today's tools are reactive dashboards or narrow scripted automations, so each product's core loop gets structurally better, not just cheaper, as multimodal reasoning, long-context memory, and native speech-to-speech models keep advancing.

I asked numerous questions about my data and the Signos app itself, receiving valuable tips on areas to focus on next.
